analysis.one_liner: Requires banks to get written permission before sharing customers' health information.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Banking Committee with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley law, banks and other financial companies can share customers' personal information with outside companies unless the customer says stop. This bill would flip that rule: companies could not share personal information with anyone, including affiliates, unless the customer first agreed in writing. Health, genetic, and medical billing information held by financial institutions would get extra protection, requiring explicit written consent. It would also ban companies from refusing service to customers who decline to share, require every financial institution to name a privacy compliance officer, and let the Justice Department seek fines of up to $100,000 per violation against companies and up to $10,000 personally against their executives and directors.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank and credit card customers, especially anyone whose financial institution holds medical, genetic, or insurance information. Today they must find an opt-out notice and act on it; under this bill nothing could be shared without their affirmative written consent, and they could not be denied a financial product for refusing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Bank customers whose data gets shared

how_it_helps.text: Requires written affirmative consent before a financial institution shares a customer's health, genetic, or medical information with anyone, including its own affiliates [S2][S3].
Prohibits a financial institution from denying a customer a product or service because the customer refused to consent to data sharing [S2][S3].
Requires every financial institution to designate a privacy compliance officer responsible for following the law and the institution's own privacy policies [S2][S3].
Lets the Attorney General sue violators for civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation, with officers and directors personally liable for up to $10,000 each [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks, credit card issuers, and other financial institutions, which would face compliance costs for tracking consent and could no longer freely monetize or share customer data. Their marketing affiliates, including insurers and data brokers, would receive less customer information. Customers would also see somewhat fewer cross-marketing offers.

drawbacks.text: The opt-in requirement is stricter than the current opt-out system, and compliance with consent tracking would impose real administrative costs on financial institutions, a burden that weighs most heavily on small community banks [S2][S3].

Requiring written consent before sharing even with a customer's own affiliates would restrict convenient services, such as streamlined account openings within a bank family, that customers may actually want [S3].
Personal civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation for officers and directors add significant liability risk for bank management [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: financial institutions often hold health and insurance-related information, and flipping the default from opt-out to opt-in meaningfully changes who controls that data. The costs are compliance expense and less cross-marketing, which is a fair trade for medical privacy, though the strict treatment of affiliate sharing and the personal penalties on executives go further than many consumers may need. On balance the bill helped ordinary customers at a cost concentrated on the financial industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 107th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Nelson introduced the bill on March 1, 2001 and spoke for it on the floor that day and again in April [S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, where it sat with no further action [S1][S5].
No other senator cosponsored the bill at any point during the two-year Congress [S4].
The bill died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, without ever coming up for a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial institutions and their marketing affiliates are better off, since they kept the opt-out data-sharing system that lets them use customer information without prior consent.

for.name: Bill Nelson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered floor remarks in its support in March and April 2001.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee of referral; controlled whether the bill advanced
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress; no hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: Financial services industry
against.role: Banks, insurers, and data brokers subject to the bill's consent and penalty requirements
against.what_they_did: Industry groups broadly opposed opt-in privacy mandates after the 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley law, arguing they would raise costs and disrupt data sharing.

sides.party_line_note: Party alignment cannot be judged from the record: the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have required written customer consent before sharing personal and health information and imposed compliance officers plus fines of up to $100,000 per violation with personal liability for executives. Its revenue from sharing and marketing customer data would shrink, which is why blocking it preserved the opt-out status quo.

industries.industry: Health and life insurers and data marketers
industries.note: These companies buy or receive financial customers' personal and health information for underwriting and marketing. The bill's opt-in rule would have cut off much of that data flow, so keeping the bill bottled up protected their access to it.
